claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claims.claim: The findings suggest greater plasticity in the life cycle than supposed.
claims.source: These findings suggest greater plasticity in the life cycle than supposed, prompting a reassessment of the current rigid view of the process.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings.

claims.claim: Slender and stumpy bloodstream stage trypanosomes can be distinguished based on cell cycle, morphological, and metabolic criteria.
claims.source: Slender and stumpy bloodstream stage trypanosomes can be distinguished based on cell cycle, morphological, and metabolic criteria.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about trypanosome biology.

claims.claim: The prescribed sequence of kinetoplast and nucleus replication (1K1N, 2K1N, 2K2N) allows cell cycle stage to be inferred.
claims.source: The genome of the single mitochondrion (kinetoplast, K) and the cell nucleus (N) can be readily visualised using DNA stains, and their prescribed sequence of replication (1K1N, 2K1N, 2K2N) allows cell cycle stage to be inferred (Sherwin and Gull, 1989).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: Slender cells are found in all three K/N ratios, while stumpy cells are found only as 1K1N cells.
claims.source: Slender cells are found in all three K/N ratios, while stumpy cells, which are cell cycle-arrested, are found only as 1K1N cells (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge illustrated by data in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: Expression of PAD1 is accepted as a marker for development to the stumpy stage.
claims.source: Expression of the protein associated with differentiation 1 (PAD1) is accepted as a marker for development to the stumpy stage (Dean et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: The 3'UTR of the PAD1 gene regulates the expression of pad1.
claims.source: As the 3'UTR of the PAD1 gene regulates the expression of pad1 (MacGregor and Matthews, 2012), cells expressing an NLS-GFP reporter fused to the 3' UTR of the PAD1 gene (GFP:PAD1UTR) will have GFP-positive nuclei when the PAD1 gene is active.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: Slender cells are GFP-negative; stumpy cells are GFP-positive when using the GFP:PAD1UTR reporter.
claims.source: Hence, slender cells are GFP-negative; stumpy cells are GFP-positive (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This is a methodological statement supported by data in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: The validity of the GFP:PAD1UTR reporter as an indicator for the activation of the PAD1 pathway has been reported previously.
claims.source: The validity of the GFP:PAD1UTR reporter as an indicator for the activation of the PAD1 pathway has been reported previously (Batram et al., 2014; Zimmermann et al., 2017), and was further corroborated by co-staining with an antibody against the PAD1 protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations and additional data in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Stumpy cells can be formed independently of high cell population density by ectopic expression of a second VSG isoform.
claims.source: We have previously shown that stumpy cells can be formed independently of high cell population density by ectopic expression of a second variant surface glycoprotein (VSG) isoform, a process that mimics one of the pathways involved in trypanosome antigenic variation (Batram et al., 2014; Cross, 1975; Hertz-Fowler et al., 2008; Zimmermann et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from previous work by the authors, supported by citations.

claims.claim: ES-attenuated stumpy cells can complete the developmental cycle in the tsetse fly.
claims.source: These so-called expression site (ES)-attenuated stumpy cells can complete the developmental cycle in the tsetse fly (Zimmermann et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from previous work, supported by citation.

claims.claim: A feeding tsetse typically ingests about 20 µl of blood.
claims.source: A feeding tsetse typically ingests about 20 µl of blood (Gibson and Bailey, 2003)
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: The uptake of just two stumpy parasites on average produced robust infections of tsetse midgut, proventriculus, and salivary glands.
claims.source: Remarkably, the uptake, on average, of just two stumpy parasites of either cell line produced robust infections of tsetse midgut (MG), proventriculus (PV), and salivary glands (SG) (Figure 1D; Figure 2A, columns 5–7, Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in multiple figures.

claims.claim: Ingestion of even a single stumpy cell on average was sufficient to produce salivary gland infections in almost 5% of all tsetse.
claims.source: Ingestion, on average, of even a single stumpy cell was sufficient to produce salivary gland infections in almost 5% of all tsetse (Figure 2A, row v).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: When the stumpy parasite number was reduced to 0.2 cells on average per bloodmeal, 0.9% of flies still acquired salivary gland infections.
claims.source: When the stumpy parasite number was further reduced to 0.2 cells on average per bloodmeal, meaning only every 5th fly would receive a stumpy cell, 0.9% of flies still acquired salivary gland infections (Figure 2A, row vi).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: The transmission index (TI) is defined as the ratio of salivary gland to midgut infections.
claims.source: The TI has been previously defined as the ratio of salivary gland to midgut infections and hence, it is a measure for successful passage through the second part of the trypanosome tsetse cycle, where trypanosomes are again infective to a mammalian host (Figures 1B, 3-5)(Peacock et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is a methodological definition supported by citation.

claims.claim: For flies infected with two trypanosomes on average, the TI was comparable between SIF-induced (TI = 0.29) and ES-induced (TI = 0.31) stumpy trypanosomes.
claims.source: We found that for flies infected with two trypanosomes on average, the TI was comparable between SIF-induced (TI = 0.29) and ES-induced (TI = 0.31) stumpy trypanosomes (Figure 2A, rows iii-iv; Figure 3).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figures 2A and 3.

claims.claim: A TI of 0.23 was observed in flies ingesting on average one trypanosome.
claims.source: A similar TI of 0.23 was observed in flies ingesting on average one trypanosome (Figure 2A, row v; Figure 3).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figures 2A and 3.

claims.claim: SIF- and ES-induced stumpy parasites are equally efficient in completing the weeks-long, multi-step fly cycle.
claims.source: Thus, our data not only clearly show that SIF- and ES-induced stumpy parasites are equally efficient in completing the weeks-long, multi-step fly cycle
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on transmission indices.

claims.claim: T. brucei infects the salivary glands, while T. congolense infects the proboscis.
claims.source: While this may seem comparable with an observation that has been made before for Trypanosoma congolense (Maudlin and Welburn, 1989), the migration through the fly differs between the two species: T. brucei infects the salivary glands, while T. congolense infects the proboscis.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about differences between trypanosome species, supported by citation.

claims.claim: The tsetse fly is much more susceptible to infections with T. congolense than with T. brucei.
claims.source: The tsetse fly, however, is much more susceptible to infections with T. congolense than with T. brucei, with a nearly 5-fold increase in percent T. congolense proboscis infections as compared to T. brucei salivary gland infections.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about differences in infection susceptibility between trypanosome species.

claims.claim: Very low numbers of T. brucei stumpy cells can successfully establish mature tsetse fly infections.
claims.source: Our results demonstrate that very low numbers of T. brucei stumpy cells can also successfully establish mature tsetse fly infections.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented.

claims.claim: Slender parasites were not only viable in the midgut, but also infected the proventriculus and the salivary glands.
claims.source: Unexpectedly, we found that slender parasites were not only viable in the midgut, but also infected the proventriculus and the salivary glands. (Figure 2A, rows vii-xi; Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figures 2A and 2B.

claims.claim: One slender parasite on average was sufficient to establish midgut infections.
claims.source: Even one slender parasite was on average sufficient to establish midgut infections, proving that slender and stumpy parasites are, in principle, equally viable in the tsetse midgut.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claims.claim: The infection efficiency was similar when flies were fed with either 20 stumpy trypanosomes or 20 pleomorphic slender trypanosomes.
claims.source: The infection efficiency, measured using TI, was similar when the flies were fed with either 20 stumpy trypanosomes or 20 pleomorphic slender trypanosomes (Figure 2A, compare TI in column eight for rows ii and vii).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: When flies were fed with an average of two slender parasites each, the TI was higher for slender cells (0.60) than for stumpy cells (0.31).
claims.source: When flies were fed with an average of two slender parasites each, the TI was actually higher for slender cells (0.60) than for stumpy cells (0.31) (Figure 3; Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 3 and supplementary figures.

claims.claim: When given, on average, just one PAD1-negative slender cell per bloodmeal, parasite infections were established in the midgut, proventriculus, and salivary glands with incidences of 4.7%, 4.1%, and 2.0% respectively, at a TI of 0.44.
claims.source: Next, when given, on average, just one PAD1-negative slender cell per bloodmeal, parasite infections were still established in the midgut, proventriculus, and salivary glands with incidences of 4.7%, 4.1%, and 2.0% respectively, at a TI of 0.44 (Figure 2A, row x; Figure 3).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figures 2A and 3.

claims.claim: Infections with, on average, two freshly-differentiated slender trypanosomes per bloodmeal revealed 6.3% midgut and 2.7% salivary gland infections with a transmission index of 0.43.
claims.source: Infections with, on average, two freshly-differentiated slender trypanosomes per bloodmeal revealed 6.3% midgut and 2.7% salivary gland infections. The transmission index was 0.43 (Figure 2A. row xiii).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Monomorphic trypanosomes are able to infect the tsetse midgut, but they are incapable of establishing robust infections and completing the developmental cycle in the fly.
claims.source: Monomorphic trypanosomes are able to infect the tsetse midgut, but they are incapable of establishing robust infections and completing the developmental cycle in the fly (Herder et al., 2007; Peacock et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: No salivary gland infections were seen using monomorphic cells, even at high infection numbers.
claims.source: As expected, no salivary gland infections were seen using these cells, even at high infection numbers.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the control experiment, consistent with established knowledge.

claims.claim: Even two monomorphic slender parasites could establish a fly midgut infection.
claims.source: Interestingly, we found that even two monomorphic slender parasites could establish a fly midgut infection (Figure 2A, row xv).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the control experiment, supported by data in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Infection of the tsetse midgut is independent of the capacity for developmental progression and the infective dose, and it does not require the stumpy life cycle stage.
claims.source: Thus, infection of the tsetse midgut is independent of the capacity for developmental progression and the infective dose, and it does not require the stumpy life cycle stage.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on monomorphic and slender infections.

claims.claim: The finding challenges the assumption that slender parasites are selectively eliminated from the parasite population and that only stumpy trypanosomes can survive the harsh conditions in the tsetse crop and midgut.
claims.source: This finding also challenges the assumption that slender parasites are selectively eliminated from the parasite population and that only stumpy trypanosomes can survive the harsh conditions thought to prevail within the tsetse crop and midgut (Nolan et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings, challenging previous assumptions supported by citation.

claims.claim: The ES-attenuated cells showed similar midgut, proventriculus, and salivary gland infection incidence as either the stumpy or slender stage.
claims.source: The ES-attenuated cells showed similar midgut, proventriculus, and salivary gland infection incidence as either the stumpy or slender stage (Figure 2A, rows ii-iii and vii-viii, Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data in Figures 2A and 2B.

claims.claim: The SIF-induced stumpy cells appeared more effective in establishing midgut infections than their slender counterparts.
claims.source: The SIF-induced stumpy cells, however, appeared more effective in establishing midgut infections than their slender counterparts (Figure 2A, rows iv-vi and ix-xi, Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data in Figures 2A and 2B.

claims.claim: The infections with one to two slender cells produced higher TI values than those with the same numbers of stumpy cells.
claims.source: First, the infections with one to two slender cells produced higher TI values than those with the same numbers of stumpy cells (Figure 3; Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data in Figure 3 and supplementary figures.

claims.claim: The proliferative slender cells are more capable of progressing from a midgut infection to a salivary gland one, and thus have at least comparable overall developmental competence to the stumpy stage.
claims.source: This suggests that the proliferative slender cells are actually more capable of progressing from a midgut infection to a salivary gland one, and thus have at least comparable overall developmental competence to the stumpy stage.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the transmission index data.

claims.claim: The lack of correlation between infective dose and midgut infections underlines the importance of the TI as a relative measure.
claims.source: Second, the lack of correlation between infective dose and midgut infections underlines the importance of the TI as a relative measure.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claims.claim: What is biologically relevant is not the initiation of infection but the completion of the tsetse passage.
claims.source: What is biologically relevant is not the initiation of infection but the completion of the tsetse passage.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the biological significance of the findings.

claims.claim: A single T. brucei cell (either slender or stumpy) can infect the tsetse fly.
claims.source: In summary, our experiments not only establish that a single T. brucei cell (either slender or stumpy) can infect the tsetse fly
claims.evidence: This is a primary conclusion supported by experimental data.

claims.claim: Infections established by slender cells can result in efficient completion of the passage through the tsetse fly.
claims.source: but also indicate that infections established by slender cells can still result in efficient completion of the passage through the tsetse fly.
claims.evidence: This is a primary conclusion supported by experimental data.

claims.claim: Ingested stumpy cells reactivate the cell cycle, begin to express the EP procyclin protein on their cell surface, and differentiate to the procyclic life cycle stage.
claims.source: The canonical version of events is that ingested stumpy (i.e. PAD1-positive) cells reactivate the cell cycle, begin to express the EP procyclin protein on their cell surface, and differentiate to the procyclic life cycle stage (Dean et al., 2009; Matthews and Gull, 1994; Mowatt and Clayton, 1987; Richardson et al., 1988; Roditi et al., 1989; Ziegelbauer and Overath, 1990).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about the canonical differentiation pathway, supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: As early as 2 hr post-infection with slender trypanosomes, 0.8% of 2K1N dividing trypanosomes with a nuclear PAD1 signal could be observed.
claims.source: As early as 2 hr post-infection with slender trypanosomes, a few (0.8%) 2K1N dividing trypanosomes with a nuclear PAD1 signal could be observed (Figure 5A, blue).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the in vivo differentiation experiment, supported by data in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: After 8 hr, half (50.4%) of all trypanosomes in the explants were PAD1-positive.
claims.source: After 8 hr however, half (38.3+6.8+5.3=50.4%) of all trypanosomes in the explants were PAD1-positive (Figure 5A; Figure 5—figure supplement 1 shows summed cell cycle category values for PAD1-positive cells).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the in vivo differentiation experiment, supported by data in Figure 5A and supplement.

claims.claim: After 24 hr, 84.3% of the parasites expressed PAD1, and 9.8% had already initiated developmental progression to the procyclic insect stage.
claims.source: After 24 hr, 84.3% (56.3+15.0+13.0) of the parasites expressed PAD1. Of these, 9.8% had already initiated developmental progression to the procyclic insect stage, as evidenced by EP1:YFP fluorescence on their cell surface (Figure 6, blue).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the in vivo differentiation experiment, supported by data in Figure 6.

claims.claim: At 48 hr post-infection with slender trypanosomes, virtually the entire trypanosome population (91.8%) expressed PAD1, and almost one fifth (19.1%) of cells were EP1-positive.
claims.source: At 48 hr post-infection with slender trypanosomes, virtually the entire trypanosome population (91.8%) expressed PAD1, and almost one fifth (19.1%) of cells were EP1-positive (Figure 6).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the in vivo differentiation experiment, supported by data in Figure 6.

claims.claim: 15 hr post-infection, the majority of all replicating (i.e. 2K1N + 2K2N) cells were PAD1-positive.
claims.source: Remarkably, 15 hr post-infection, the majority of all replicating (i.e. 2K1N + 2K2N) cells were PAD1-positive (Figure 5B; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the in vivo differentiation experiment, supported by data in Figure 5B and supplement.

claims.claim: No indication of a transient cell cycle arrest or intermittent impairment of cell cycle progression was observed in slender cells during differentiation.
claims.source: No indication of a transient cell cycle arrest or intermittent impairment of cell cycle progression was observed.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the in vivo differentiation experiment.

claims.claim: After 2 days, more than 90% of dividing trypanosomes were PAD1-positive.
claims.source: After 2 days, more than 90% of dividing trypanosomes were PAD1-positive.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the in vivo differentiation experiment.

claims.claim: The PAD1 pathway was triggered in replicating slender trypanosomes upon ingestion by the fly, without prior or subsequent cell cycle arrest.
claims.source: Thus, the PAD1 pathway was triggered in replicating slender trypanosomes upon ingestion by the fly, without prior or subsequent cell cycle arrest.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the in vivo differentiation data.

claims.claim: Stumpy trypanosomes remained as 1K1N cells in cell cycle arrest for the first day after uptake by the tsetse fly, then differentiated to procyclic cells and re-entered the cell cycle after 2 days.
claims.source: These cells remained as 1K1N cells in cell cycle arrest for the first day, then differentiated to procyclic cells and re-entered the cell cycle after 2 days.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the in vivo differentiation experiment comparing stumpy to slender cells.

claims.claim: Four hours after uptake by the tsetse fly, stumpy trypanosomes started expressing EP1:YFP.
claims.source: Four hours after uptake by the tsetse fly, stumpy trypanosomes started expressing EP1:YFP (Figure 6, red).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the in vivo differentiation experiment, supported by data in Figure 6.

claims.claim: The fluorescent reporter was visible on 16.2% of stumpy cells after 10 hr, showing that EP expression was initiated before release of cell cycle arrest.
claims.source: The fluorescent reporter was visible on 16.2% of stumpy cells after 10 hr, showing that EP expression was initiated before release of cell cycle arrest (Figure 5C, red; Figure 6, red).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the in vivo differentiation experiment, supported by data in Figures 5C and 6.

claims.claim: Uncoupling of EP surface expression from the commitment to differentiation has been reported before.
claims.source: Uncoupling of EP surface expression from the commitment to differentiation has been reported before (Engstler and Boshart, 2004).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: EP1:YFP expression in slender parasites lagged 12 hr behind stumpy cells, only becoming widespread after 24 hr.
claims.source: EP1:YFP expression in slender parasites lagged 12 hr behind stumpy cells, only becoming widespread after 24 hr (Figure 6).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the in vivo differentiation experiment, supported by data in Figure 6.

claims.claim: The onset of EP1 expression was shifted, but the kinetics of differentiation were comparable in slender and stumpy parasites.
claims.source: Thus, the onset of EP1 expression was shifted, but the kinetics of differentiation were comparable in slender and stumpy parasites
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the in vivo differentiation data.

claims.claim: Activation of the PAD1 pathway preceded developmental progression in slender cells.
claims.source: and activation of the PAD1 pathway also preceded developmental progression in slender cells.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the in vivo differentiation experiment.

claims.claim: Expression of PAD1 is essential for differentiation to the procyclic stage, while cell cycle arrest is not.
claims.source: This strongly suggests that expression of PAD1 is essential for differentiation to the procyclic stage, while cell cycle arrest is not.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that slender cells can differentiate without cell cycle arrest.

claims.claim: EP1 expression did not directly correlate with acquisition of procyclic morphology.
claims.source: Of note, EP1 expression did not directly correlate with acquisition of procyclic morphology.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the in vivo differentiation experiment.

claims.claim: At 24 hr, 9.8% of slender cells were EP1-positive, but EP1-negative cells frequently exhibited procyclic morphology.
claims.source: At 24 hr, 9.8% of slender cells were EP1-positive (Figure 6), but the EP1-negative cells frequently exhibited procyclic morphology (Figure 4, upper panels).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the in vivo differentiation experiment, supported by data in Figures 4 and 6.

claims.claim: GPEET is another procyclic surface protein that is expressed early in the transition from bloodstream stage to procyclic stage cells in the tsetse midgut, before being replaced by EP.
claims.source: GPEET is another procyclic surface protein that is expressed early in the transition from bloodstream stage to procyclic stage cells in the tsetse midgut, before being replaced by EP (Vassella et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: A seamless developmental stage transition from the slender bloodstream stage to the procyclic insect stage took place, accompanied by re-organisation of the cytoskeleton and the concomitant switch of swimming styles.
claims.source: This strongly suggests that a seamless developmental stage transition from the slender bloodstream stage to the procyclic insect stage took place, which was accompanied by the typical re-organisation of the cytoskeleton and the concomitant switch of swimming styles (Rotureau et al., 2011; Heddergott et al., 2012; Schuster et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observations, supported by citations to previous work on morphological changes.

claims.claim: In the laboratory, differentiation to the procyclic insect stage is routinely induced by the addition of cis-aconitate, removal of glucose, and a temperature drop from 37°C to 27°C.
claims.source: In the laboratory, differentiation to the procyclic insect stage is routinely induced by the addition of cis-aconitate, removal of glucose, and a temperature drop from 37°C to 27°C (Brun et al., 1981; Czichos et al., 1986; Engstler and Boshart, 2004; Qiu et al., 2018; Ziegelbauer et al., 1990).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about laboratory methods, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Slender trypanosomes activated the PAD1 pathway rapidly after receiving the differentiation trigger in vitro, with 9.8% of all parasites being PAD1-positive within 2 hr, and 83.2% after 10 hr.
claims.source: Slender trypanosomes activated the PAD1 pathway rapidly after receiving the trigger, with 9.8% of all parasites being PAD1-positive within 2 hr, and 83.2% after 10 hr.

claims.source: Shortly after PAD1 reporter expression, EP1 appeared on the cell surface of 19.6% of all parasites within 8 hr, increasing to 98.3% after 3 days (Figure 8).

claims.claim: PAD1-positive slender parasites did not arrest in the cell cycle during in vitro differentiation, and continued dividing throughout.

claims.source: By comparison, stumpy parasites (Figure 7A, red) responded to in vitro cis-aconitate treatment with rapid expression of the EP1:YFP marker, with 28.6% of all cells being positive within 2 hr (Figure 8).

claims.claim: After 1 day of in vitro differentiation, EP1 was present on almost all (96.7%) stumpy trypanosomes.
claims.source: After 1 day, EP1 was present on almost all (96.7%) stumpy trypanosomes.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the in vitro differentiation experiment.

claims.claim: Stumpy parasites were not dividing during the first day of in vitro differentiation.

claims.evidence: This is a finding from the in vitro differentiation experiment, supported by data in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: The first stumpy cells re-entered the cell cycle only after 15 hr during in vitro differentiation, and a normal procyclic cell cycle profile was not reached until day 3.
claims.source: The first cells re-entered the cell cycle only after 15 hr, and a normal procyclic cell cycle profile was not reached until day 3.

claims.source: To summarise, the overall developmental capacity of the two life cycle stages - slender and stumpy cells - is comparable both in vitro and in vivo.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined in vitro and in vivo differentiation data.

results.result: A single trypanosome is sufficient to establish productive tsetse fly infection. Experiments showed that on average, ingestion of just two stumpy parasites produced robust infections of tsetse midgut, proventriculus, and salivary glands. Even a single stumpy cell on average was sufficient to produce salivary gland infections in almost 5% of tsetse, and when reduced to 0.2 cells per bloodmeal, 0.9% of flies still acquired salivary gland infections.
results.evaluation: Claims C39, C52-C54, C80, and C117 are well-supported by systematic quantitative data presented in Figure 2A showing infection rates at various parasite doses. The experimental design includes appropriate controls (monomorphic parasites), multiple replicates, and clear dose-response relationships. The transmission index (TI) provides a validated measure of successful life cycle completion.

results.result: Slender stage trypanosomes can infect tsetse flies and complete the full developmental cycle with comparable or superior efficiency to stumpy stages. Slender parasites infected midgut, proventriculus, and salivary glands. When flies were fed with an average of two slender parasites, the transmission index (TI) was higher for slender cells (0.60) than stumpy cells (0.31). Even one slender parasite on average established infections with a TI of 0.44.
results.evaluation: Claims C40, C63-C68, C81, C118-C119, C149, and C151 are strongly supported by experimental data in Figures 2A, 2B, and 3. Multiple independent experiments with different slender cell preparations (including freshly differentiated cells from metacyclics, C68) demonstrate reproducibility. The higher TI for slender cells at low doses (C66, C76) is particularly compelling evidence challenging the traditional dogma.

results.result: SIF-induced and ES-induced stumpy parasites are equally efficient in completing the tsetse fly cycle. For flies infected with two trypanosomes on average, the TI was comparable between SIF-induced (0.29) and ES-induced (0.31) stumpy trypanosomes, with a similar TI of 0.23 observed for flies ingesting one trypanosome on average.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C58 and C62 are supported by quantitative data in Figures 2A and 3 comparing the two stumpy induction methods. The comparable TI values demonstrate that the ES-attenuation method produces functionally equivalent stumpy cells to SIF induction, validating this experimental approach and ruling out method-specific artifacts.

results.result: Monomorphic trypanosomes can establish midgut infections but cannot complete the developmental cycle. No salivary gland infections were observed with monomorphic cells even at high doses, but even two monomorphic slender parasites could establish midgut infection. This demonstrates that midgut infection is independent of developmental competence and does not require the stumpy stage.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C73 are supported by control experiments with monomorphic parasites (Figure 2A, rows xiii-xv). The ability of monomorphic cells to establish midgut but not salivary gland infections provides important negative controls demonstrating that initial survival in the midgut is distinct from developmental progression. This challenges previous assumptions about selective elimination of slender parasites (C73).

results.result: Stumpy stages appear more effective at establishing initial midgut infections, while slender-derived parasites produce salivary gland infections more efficiently (higher TI). SIF-induced stumpy cells showed higher midgut infection rates than slender counterparts, but infections with one to two slender cells produced higher TI values than stumpy cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C77, C120-C121 are supported by comparative data in Figures 2A-B and Figure 3. The differential performance at midgut establishment versus progression to salivary glands is an important nuanced finding. However, the interpretation (C77) that slender cells have "at least comparable overall developmental competence" is reasonable given the higher TI values, though the biological mechanism remains speculative.

results.result: In the tsetse midgut, slender trypanosomes activate the PAD1 pathway and differentiate to procyclic stage without cell cycle arrest. As early as 2 hr post-infection, 0.8% of dividing (2K1N) slender cells showed PAD1 signal. By 8 hr, 50.4% were PAD1-positive, reaching 91.8% by 48 hr. Remarkably, at 15 hr post-infection, the majority of replicating cells were PAD1-positive with no indication of cell cycle arrest.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C83-C90, and C97 are strongly supported by in vivo time-course data in Figures 5A-B and Figure 6. The observation of PAD1-positive dividing cells (C87) is particularly important, directly demonstrating that PAD1 activation occurs without cell cycle arrest. The large sample sizes (n=1845 slender cells) and multiple timepoints provide robust evidence. Statistical modeling (GAM) appropriately accounts for temporal dynamics.

results.result: Stumpy trypanosomes remain cell cycle-arrested for the first day after tsetse uptake, then differentiate to procyclic cells. Stumpy cells remained as 1K1N cells in cell cycle arrest for the first day, started expressing EP1:YFP after 4 hr (16.2% by 10 hr), and re-entered the cell cycle after 2 days. EP1:YFP expression in slender parasites lagged 12 hr behind stumpy cells, but differentiation kinetics were comparable.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C93, C95-C96 are supported by in vivo time-course data in Figures 5C and 6 (n=1237 stumpy cells). The delayed cell cycle re-entry in stumpy cells contrasts with continuous division in slender cells, highlighting a key mechanistic difference. The observation that EP expression precedes cell cycle re-entry (C93) is consistent with prior literature (C94) and validates the experimental approach.

results.result: PAD1 pathway activation is essential for differentiation to procyclic stage, while cell cycle arrest is not. The observation that slender cells differentiate without cell cycle arrest, and that EP1 surface expression correlates with PAD1 activation in both cell types, strongly suggests PAD1 is essential but cell cycle arrest is dispensable.
results.evaluation: Claims C98, C115, and C150 represent key mechanistic inferences well-supported by the combined in vivo data (Figures 5-6). The logic is sound: if slender cells can differentiate while dividing (C90) but always activate PAD1 first (C97), then PAD1 is necessary but cell cycle arrest is not. The correlation between PAD1 activation and EP1 surface access (C115) provides additional mechanistic support.

results.result: In vitro differentiation experiments confirm that slender trypanosomes can directly differentiate to procyclic stage without cell cycle arrest. Upon cis-aconitate treatment, slender cells rapidly activated PAD1 (83.2% by 10 hr, peaking at 98.3% by 24 hr), followed by EP1 expression (19.6% by 8 hr, 98.3% by 3 days). PAD1-positive slender cells continued dividing throughout differentiation, establishing a proliferating procyclic population by 3 days.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C108 and C113 are supported by in vitro time-course data in Figures 7A-B, 8, and morphological analysis (Figure 7 supplement 3). The in vitro results (n=1653 slender cells) corroborate the in vivo findings, demonstrating that the phenomenon is not specific to the tsetse midgut environment. The continuous presence of PAD1-positive dividing cells (C107) directly parallels the in vivo observations, strengthening the overall conclusion.

results.result: In vitro, stumpy parasites rapidly express EP1 but remain cell cycle-arrested initially. Stumpy cells responded to cis-aconitate with rapid EP1:YFP expression (28.6% by 2 hr, 96.7% by 24 hr) but were not dividing during the first day. Cell cycle re-entry began only after 15 hr, with normal procyclic cell cycle profile not reached until day 3.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C112 are supported by in vitro data in Figures 7C and 8 (n=1798 stumpy cells). These results parallel the in vivo stumpy differentiation kinetics, demonstrating consistency between experimental systems. The delayed cell cycle re-entry contrasts with the continuous division of slender cells, reinforcing the key mechanistic difference between the two pathways.

results.result: The overall developmental capacity of slender and stumpy cells is comparable both in vitro and in vivo.
results.evaluation: Claim C116 is a summary conclusion well-supported by the combined in vivo (Figures 5-6) and in vitro (Figures 7-8) differentiation data. Both cell types successfully differentiate to procyclic stage with similar kinetics (though different mechanisms), and both can complete the full tsetse life cycle (Figures 2-3). This represents a major conceptual advance in understanding trypanosome biology.

results.result: EP1 expression does not directly correlate with acquisition of procyclic morphology. At 24 hr in vivo, only 9.8% of slender cells were EP1-positive, but EP1-negative cells frequently exhibited procyclic morphology.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C100 are supported by observations in Figures 4 and 6. This finding suggests that morphological changes can precede EP1 surface expression, possibly due to earlier expression of GPEET (C101). However, the manuscript acknowledges that GPEET expression was not directly assessed, representing a limitation. The observation is consistent with prior work showing uncoupling of EP expression from differentiation commitment (C94).

results.result: The findings demonstrate greater plasticity in the trypanosome life cycle than previously supposed, challenging the rigid view of the process.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C41, C157-C158 represent high-level conclusions well-supported by the experimental findings. The demonstration that slender cells can complete the life cycle (C7, C40, C119) and differentiate without cell cycle arrest (C90, C113) directly contradicts the traditional rigid model requiring stumpy stage formation. This represents a paradigm shift in understanding trypanosome transmission biology.

results.result: The findings may provide a solution to the transmission paradox—the successful transmission of parasites in chronic infections despite low parasitemia—without challenging existing work on stumpy trypanosomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C10, C148, and C159 represent speculative interpretations about field implications. While the demonstration that single slender cells can infect flies (C39, C80) provides a plausible mechanism for transmission at low parasitemia, direct evidence linking these laboratory findings to field transmission dynamics is lacking. The manuscript appropriately frames these as possibilities ("may provide") rather than definitive solutions. Additional field studies would be needed to validate this hypothesis.

results.result: Based on Koch's historical data, an average blood parasitemia of 10-100 trypanosomes/ml can be calculated, meaning two or fewer trypanosomes would be present in an average tsetse bloodmeal.
results.evaluation: Claims C128-C129 are supported by calculations based on historical data from Koch (1909) presented in Appendix 1. Given that a tsetse bloodmeal is ~20 µl (C51), the arithmetic is straightforward. However, the accuracy depends on the reliability of Koch's century-old parasitemia estimates and whether they represent typical chronic infections. The calculation provides useful historical context but should be interpreted cautiously.

results.result: The essential biological function of the stumpy stage in T. brucei may be quorum sensing-dependent control of population size in the host rather than transmission. Density-dependent differentiation at the population level may be a later evolutionary innovation specific to the T. brucei group.
results.evaluation: Claims C153 and C156 represent speculative evolutionary interpretations. While the experimental data demonstrate that stumpy stage is not uniquely required for transmission (C118, C151), this does not definitively establish what the "essential" function is. The comparison to T. congolense (C152, C155) provides some comparative context, but evolutionary inferences require additional phylogenetic and functional data. These remain plausible hypotheses requiring further investigation.

results.result: Slender trypanosomes exhibit significantly higher motility than stumpy trypanosomes, and glucose levels are a developmental trigger in addition to cold shock and cis-aconitate.
results.evaluation: Claims C122-C123 cite established knowledge from the literature (Bargul et al., 2016; Qiu et al., 2018). These are not new findings from this study but provide important context for interpreting the results. The higher motility of slender cells (C122) is used to speculate about their higher TI values (discussion), though this hypothesis is not directly tested.

results.result: Stumpy cells have a limited lifespan (~3 days) and require at least one day to re-enter the cell cycle in the fly, meaning only young stumpy cells would be successful. The experiments used only freshly differentiated stumpy cells, thus overestimating their success rate under natural conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C142-C147 combine established knowledge (C142: Turner et al., 1995) with findings from this study (C143: Figure 5C, 7C) and logical inferences (C144-C145, C147). The reasoning is sound: if stumpy cells live ~3 days and need 1 day to re-enter the cell cycle, then cells older than ~2 days would likely fail. The acknowledgment that experiments used fresh stumpy cells (C146) is an important limitation, suggesting the study may actually overestimate stumpy cell success in natural infections.

results.result: The lack of correlation between infective dose and midgut infections underlines the importance of the transmission index (TI) as a relative measure. What is biologically relevant is not the initiation of infection but the completion of the tsetse passage.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C79 represent methodological and conceptual insights supported by the data patterns in Figure 2A. The observation that midgut infection rates vary inconsistently with dose while TI values show clearer patterns supports the interpretation that TI is a more meaningful metric. This is an important conceptual point for evaluating transmission competence, though the biological mechanisms underlying the dose-response patterns remain unclear.
